Ethereum finalizes the chain by having validators vote on blocks with staked ETH at stake. If an attacker holds more than half of the total stake, they can censor by continually delaying certain transactions, and if they hold close to two thirds, they can even attempt to revert blocks that have already been finalized.

There are defenses today. Reverting finality requires casting contradictory votes, and doing so carries a penalty (slashing) that costs a large part of the stake. If more than one third of validators stop voting so that finality cannot be reached, the inactivity leak gradually reduces the stake of the side that stopped, and the remaining validators resume finalizing.

However, there is no automatic response inside the protocol to censorship in which a majority votes but leaves out certain transactions. Today the community must confirm the attack and manually coordinate a minority fork that does not follow the attacker's chain. This is slow, and the judgment of who the attacker is is also left to people.

This item is research aimed at bringing that detection and response into the protocol as far as possible. The specific method has not been decided, and it sits in the furthest long-term column of the Strawmap, so its content may change.

BLS relies on elliptic curve mathematics, and it is known that once a sufficiently large quantum computer exists, the private key can be derived from the public key. The two programs also connect to other nodes in different ways. The execution client uses devp2p, which has been in use since 2015, and the consensus client uses libp2p, which was chosen when the Beacon Chain was designed. With The Merge in 2022 the two chains became one, but the networking remained split in two.

Two networking systems mean twice the work. Client teams must maintain two kinds of network code and review security issues separately. A team building a new client must implement both systems. A single node also manages two peer lists.

Ethereum's consensus layer (the beacon chain) launched in late 2020 and has since layered change upon change, such as the Merge, withdrawals and validator structure improvements. Because it was safer to add new rules on top of existing ones than to delete them, structures that are no longer used or that were built for earlier circumstances remain throughout the spec and client code. In software, this accumulated burden is called tech debt. A complex spec increases the places where bugs can hide and makes it harder for new client teams to take part. It is also an obstacle when trying to verify the consensus process with zero-knowledge proofs.

This item proposes cleaning up that debt all at once instead of fixing it bit by bit. The idea of clearing the accumulated debt while redesigning the consensus layer came from the Beam chain (now called lean consensus) concept that Ethereum Foundation researcher Justin Drake presented at Devcon 2024. On the Strawmap it sits in the same cell as one-round finality, attester-proposer separation and real-time CL proving. These changes will greatly alter the core of the consensus layer anyway, so the judgment is that removing the old structures at the same time yields a simpler design that is easier to prove. However, the L* fork is only an estimate on the Strawmap, and what to clean up and how far has not yet been decided.

In Ethereum today, which validator will propose a block in which slot is decided before an epoch (a group of 32 slots) begins. Anyone can see that list. An attacker can look at the list and flood the next proposer's node with traffic so that it cannot produce a block. If such a denial-of-service (DoS) attack succeeds, that slot is empty and transactions are delayed. It also creates room for the next proposer to take the fee revenue for that slot. The fact that the proposer is known in advance is itself the starting point for targeted attacks.

A secret proposer hides this list. Only the proposer knows its own turn. Only at the moment the block is published does the network confirm that the person was a legitimate proposer. This makes it harder to pick a specific validator in advance and attack it, and it makes small solo validators safer. In the Ethereum research community this approach is called secret leader election. Designs such as Whisk, which uses a shuffle that mixes commitments together with zero-knowledge proofs, have been proposed. In the Strawmap it sits in the long-term column with no assigned fork, so which upgrade it will go into has not yet been decided.

The fee schedule is based on values set in the early days, and although it has been adjusted several times since, it has not kept pace with changes in hardware and network conditions.
